latest_release.body:
## [10.5.0](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/compare/v10.4.1...v10.5.0) (2026-11-10)

<!-- release-notes:start -->

### Summary

Adds per-message cancellation to `sendMail()` with an AbortSignal, plus two encoding fixes: DKIM signatures for internationalized domains, and header text that looks like a broken encoded-word.

### Who should upgrade

- Anyone who signs with DKIM for a domain written with upper case or mapped non-ASCII characters (an upper case IDN label, or one holding a soft hyphen). The `d=` tag named a different domain than `From:`, so verification and DMARC alignment failed.
- Anyone who wants to cancel or time-limit a single send without closing the transport or pool.

### Highlights

- **AbortSignal per send:** `sendMail({ ..., signal })` on SMTP and pooled SMTP. An abort removes a queued message from the pool, or closes only the connection delivering it, and the send fails with an `AbortError` (code `EABORT`). Other transports honor a signal that is already aborted and otherwise ignore it. Note that an abort late in DATA does not prove the server did not accept the message, so do not treat `EABORT` as safe to retry blindly.
- **DKIM:** the `d=` domain is encoded with UTS-46 mapping, the same way as the address headers.
- **Header encoding:** plain text that a receiver would decode as an encoded-word without it being a valid one (such as `=?utf-8?Q?a b?=` across a space) is now encoded. A valid encoded-word is still passed through, so subjects that are already encoded are not encoded twice.
- **SMTP connection:** a supplied socket no longer connects, and TLS no longer starts, after the connection was closed.

<!-- release-notes:end -->


### Features

* **smtp:** support AbortSignal for individual sends ([#1911](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/issues/1911)) ([66387ed](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/66387ed6f4bd26208b944b74b7329201ad77377b)), closes [#1910](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/issues/1910)


### Bug Fixes

* **dkim:** encode the d= domain the same way as the address headers ([#1908](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/issues/1908)) ([4ebf03f](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/4ebf03fba33a96118c10afa340ce895a00549148))
* **mime-funcs:** encode header text that would be decoded as an invalid encoded word ([#1912](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/issues/1912)) ([7a7b942](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/7a7b9427b632d8785190747ae2c62e88e77bc837))

detail.readme:
# Nodemailer

[![Nodemailer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/master/assets/nm_logo_200x136.png)](https://nodemailer.com/about/)

Send emails from Node.js – easy as cake! 🍰✉️

[![NPM](https://nodei.co/npm/nodemailer.png?downloads=true&downloadRank=true&stars=true)](https://nodemailer.com/about/)

See [nodemailer.com](https://nodemailer.com/) for documentation and terms.

> Nodemailer is developed by the team behind **[EmailEngine](https://emailengine.app/?utm_source=nodemailer-readme&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=oss-docs)**, a self-hosted email API that turns any Gmail, Microsoft 365, or IMAP account into a REST endpoint, with managed OAuth2, webhooks for incoming mail, and built-in [sending](https://emailengine.app/sending-emails?utm_source=nodemailer-readme&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=oss-docs). If you would rather call an HTTP API than maintain IMAP and SMTP connections yourself, that is what it is for.

## Supported runtimes

Nodemailer targets Node.js 20 and later. The ES module build also runs on [Bun](https://bun.sh/) (tested against the latest release) and on [Cloudflare Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/) with the `nodejs_compat` compatibility flag. On Workers only the SMTP based transports apply, `sendmail` needs a child process, and the runtime does not allow turning certificate validation off, so `tls.rejectUnauthorized: false` fails there with an error.

## Cancelling an individual SMTP send

Pass an `AbortSignal` in the message options to cancel one `sendMail()` call:

```js
await transporter.sendMail({
    from: 'sender@example.com',
    to: 'recipient@example.com',
    text: 'Hello',
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)
});
```

This is supported by SMTP and pooled SMTP transports. A pre-aborted signal prevents processing; aborting later stops subsequent plugin processing, removes a queued message, or closes the SMTP connection assigned to that message. Other deliveries in the pool can continue. Both promise and callback forms report an error named `AbortError`, with `code: 'EABORT'` and the signal's reason as `cause`. The signal listener is removed when the send finishes.

Cancellation stops local processing; it does not prove that the SMTP server has not already accepted the message. Do not retry a cancelled send automatically on that assumption.

Work already started by a plugin or a custom `getSocket` hook requires that code's cooperation to stop. Nodemailer ignores late plugin completion and destroys a socket handed back after cancellation. Plugins can read `mail.data.signal` to cancel their own work.

Other bundled transports (stream, JSON, sendmail and SES) ignore the signal once the message is handed to them, so the message is sent normally. A signal that is already aborted, or aborts while plugins run, still cancels the send with `EABORT` on every transport, as that happens before the transport is called. A `signal` value that is not an `AbortSignal` fails the send with `ECONFIG`. Custom transports can opt in with `supportsAbortSignal: true`; their `send()` must register its abort listener synchronously, check for a pre-aborted signal, stop the work it owns, invoke its callback once, and remove the listener on completion.

## SMTP socket close timeout

When an SMTP connection closes, Nodemailer ends the socket and destroys it if the server has not closed its side within `socketCloseTimeout` milliseconds (default 5000). Set it to `0` to destroy the socket right away. This applies to SMTP and pooled SMTP, including aborted sends and `transporter.close({ force: true })`. It does not tell you whether the server accepted a message that was in flight.

## Having an issue?

#### First review the docs

Documentation for Nodemailer can be found at [nodemailer.com](https://nodemailer.com/about/).

#### Nodemailer fails to load or throws a SyntaxError

Nodemailer 10 and later require Node.js 20 or newer. The package ships both ES module and CommonJS builds, so `import nodemailer from 'nodemailer'` and `const nodemailer = require('nodemailer')` both work. If you need to run on an older Node.js version, stay on the 9.x line.

#### I'm having issues with Gmail

Gmail either works well, or it does not work at all. It is probably easier to switch to an alternative service instead of fixing issues with Gmail. If Gmail does not work for you, then don't use it. Read more about it [here](https://nodemailer.com/usage/using-gmail/). If the blocker is OAuth2 setup rather than Gmail itself, [EmailEngine](https://emailengine.app/?utm_source=nodemailer-readme&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=oss-docs&utm_content=faq-gmail) handles the OAuth2 flow and token refresh for you.

#### I get ETIMEDOUT errors

Check your firewall settings. Timeout usually occurs when you try to open a connection to a firewalled port either on the server or on your machine. Some ISPs also block email ports to prevent spamming.

#### Nodemailer works on one machine but not in another

It's either a firewall issue, or your SMTP server blocks authentication attempts from some servers.

#### I get TLS errors

- If you are running the code on your machine, check your antivirus settings. Antiviruses often mess around with email ports usage. Node.js might not recognize the MITM cert your antivirus is using.
- Latest Node versions allow only TLS versions 1.2 and higher. Some servers might still use TLS 1.1 or lower. Check Node.js docs on how to get correct TLS support for your app. You can change this with [tls.minVersion](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v16.x/docs/api/tls.html#tls_tls_createsecurecontext_options) option
- You might have the wrong value for the `secure` option. This should be set to `true` only for port 465. For every other port, it should be `false`. Setting it to `false` does not mean that Nodemailer would not use TLS. Nodemailer would still try to upgrade the connection to use TLS if the server supports it.
- Older Node versions do not fully support the certificate chain of the newest Let's Encrypt certificates. Either set [tls.rejectUnauthorized](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v16.x/docs/api/tls.html#tlsconnectoptions-callback) to `false` to skip chain verification or upgrade your Node version

```js
let configOptions = {
    host: 'smtp.example.com',
    port: 587,
    tls: {
        rejectUnauthorized: true,
        minVersion: 'TLSv1.2'
    }
};
```

#### I have issues with DNS / hosts file

Node.js uses [c-ares](https://github.com/c-ares/c-ares) to resolve domain names, not the DNS library provided by the system, so if you have some custom DNS routing set up, it might be ignored. Nodemailer runs [dns.resolve4()](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v16.x/docs/api/dns.html#dnsresolve4hostname-options-callback) and [dns.resolve6()](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v16.x/docs/api/dns.html#dnsresolve6hostname-options-callback) to resolve hostname into an IP address. If both calls fail, then Nodemailer will fall back to [dns.lookup()](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v16.x/docs/api/dns.html#dnslookuphostname-options-callback). If this does not work for you, you can hard code the IP address into the configuration like shown below. In that case, Nodemailer would not perform any DNS lookups.

```js
let configOptions = {
    host: '1.2.3.4',
    port: 465,
    secure: true,
    tls: {
        // must provide server name, otherwise TLS certificate check will fail
        servername: 'example.com'
    }
};
```

#### I have an issue with TypeScript types

Nodemailer 10 and later are written in TypeScript and ship their own type definitions, so `@types/nodemailer` is no longer needed and should be removed from your project to avoid conflicting declarations. The type names follow the layout of the old definitions, so references such as `Mail.Options`, `SMTPTransport.Options` or `Transporter<SMTPTransport.SentMessageInfo>` keep compiling, and the most used types (`SendMailOptions`, `Transporter`, `SentMessageInfo`, `Attachment`, `Address`) are exported from the package root. The modules under `nodemailer/lib/` are declared with a default export, so import a class as `import SMTPTransport from 'nodemailer/lib/smtp-transport'` (with `esModuleInterop` in a CommonJS project). The `import SMTPTransport = require(...)` and `import * as SMTPTransport from ...` forms still resolve the type aliases such as `SMTPTransport.Options`, but they refer to the module rather than to the class, so the class itself has to be imported with a default import. For older Nodemailer versions, the community maintained [type definitions](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@types/nodemailer) still apply.

#### I have a different problem

If you are having issues with Nodemailer, then the best way to find help would be [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/search?q=nodemailer) or revisit the [docs](https://nodemailer.com/about/).
